companies.name: Amazon
companies.tagline: The most heavily documented hiring process in tech: a published OA structure, a published decision SLA, and 16 Leadership Principles that every interviewer scores you against.
companies.transparencyNote: Amazon publishes more about its own interview process than any other company on this site: exact OA section timings, loop length, decision deadlines, the Bar Raiser programme and all 16 Leadership Principles in their own words. Almost everything on this page is a direct company statement. The two things Amazon does not publish are stage pass rates and whether the Bar Raiser holds a formal veto.

What is an Amazon Bar Raiser?
Amazon interview process: from phone screens to interview loops
How 3 AI innovations are creating a better experience for candidates in Amazon hiring

hiringPhilosophy.value: Amazon optimises for hire quality over hire speed, and asks every loop to decide whether the candidate raises the bar rather than merely clears it. Its published pipeline is: online application, assessments, phone screening, interview loop.
hiringPhilosophy.quote: Amazon is focused on hiring well, rather than hiring quickly.

levels.title: Software Development Engineer I
levels.primaryExpectation: Write correct, readable code for a well-scoped problem; reason about time and space complexity out loud; bring concrete STAR examples even from coursework and internships.

levels.title: Software Development Engineer II
levels.primaryExpectation: Own a service end to end. Amazon states the SDE II loop is four 55-minute interviews and that you should expect at least one software systems design question.

levels.title: Senior Software Development Engineer
levels.primaryExpectation: Design across team boundaries, handle ambiguity, and evidence a track record against the harder Leadership Principles - Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit, Think Big, Dive Deep.

totalRounds.value: One or two phone interviews, then a loop. For SDE II the loop is four 55-minute interviews.
totalRounds.quote: four 55-minute interviews where you'll meet with members of our software development community

averageHiringTimeline.value: Three to six weeks on average, with a published decision SLA at each gate.
averageHiringTimeline.quote: On average, the process takes between three and six weeks.

platformClaim.value: Amazon points candidates at a sample challenge on HackerRank for the online assessment coding section.

durationClaim.value: Full-time SDE: set aside up to two hours of uninterrupted time. Internship OA is about 90 minutes and drops the Work Simulation.
durationClaim.quote: set aside up to two hours of uninterrupted time for the OA

sections.name: Coding Assessment
sections.description: The algorithmic section. Amazon publishes the average time rather than a hard cap.

sections.name: Workstyles Assessment
sections.description: Forced-choice statements mapped to the Leadership Principles. Present in both the full-time and internship OA.

sections.name: Work Simulation
sections.description: Scenario-based day-in-the-life exercise. Full-time only - the internship OA does not include it.

sectionsClaim.value: Amazon publishes the OA as four parts with average times: Coding 70 min, Workstyles 15 min, Work Simulation 60 min, Feedback Survey 5 min.

proctoring.value: Amazon warns that using print screen terminates the session, and tells candidates to avoid copying and pasting inside the assessment.
proctoring.quote: Do not use the print screen functionality, because your session will be terminated

tips.value: Review and practise the coding language you plan to use before you start.
If you get stuck, move to the next question and come back - the assessment allows revisiting.
Practise coding outside an IDE. Amazon says so directly, and both the OA and the whiteboard rounds remove autocomplete.
tips.quote: reviewing computer science fundamentals and practicing coding outside of an integrated development environment

tips.value: Treat the Workstyles Assessment as a Leadership Principles exam rather than a personality test: choose the answer that most clearly demonstrates Customer Obsession, Ownership and Dive Deep rather than the balanced middle option.
tips.note: Amazon publishes no scoring key for the Workstyles Assessment. This reflects widely repeated candidate guidance, not a company statement.

roadmapStages.title: Application and resume review
roadmapStages.description: Amazon uses machine learning to match candidates to roles rather than pure keyword matching, and says candidates matched this way who reach interview are 24% more likely to get a positive outcome.

timeframe.note: Amazon publishes no target time for resume review. Its published SLAs start at the phone screen.

keyMilestones: Resume parsed and matched against open requisitions
Recruiter or Candidate Partner makes first contact
Online assessment invitation for most SDE pipelines
checklistItems: Quantify impact in each bullet - Amazon describes itself as a data-driven company and tells candidates to bring metrics
Name the distributed-systems and cloud work explicitly; Amazon lists distributed computing as an interview topic
Single-column PDF so the parser reads it cleanly

roadmapStages.title: Online assessment
roadmapStages.description: Four-part assessment. The coding section now puts candidates on a real coding platform with an interactive AI assistant, which Amazon announced in January 2026.

timeframe.value: Up to two hours of uninterrupted time.

keyMilestones: Work Simulation (average 60 minutes, full-time roles only)
checklistItems: Do not use print screen - it terminates the session
Avoid copy and paste inside the assessment
Have a quiet uninterrupted two-hour block booked

roadmapStages.title: Phone screen
roadmapStages.description: One or two phone interviews over Amazon Chime or Zoom. Amazon says phone screens often assess basic qualifications.

timeframe.value: Amazon targets an update within two business days after the phone interview.
timeframe.quote: Our goal is to provide an update within two business days after your phone interview

keyMilestones: Live coding in a shared editor
checklistItems: Test Amazon Chime and Zoom in advance - Amazon names both
Decide your interview-transcription preference in your profile beforehand; it is voluntary and does not affect evaluation
Have two STAR stories ready per Leadership Principle you expect to be asked about

roadmapStages.title: The loop
roadmapStages.description: For SDE II, four 55-minute interviews. Across the whole process you can meet anywhere from two to seven Amazon employees, and one interviewer in the loop is a Bar Raiser from outside the hiring team.

timeframe.value: Amazon targets an update within five business days after the loop.
timeframe.quote: within five business days after your interview loop

keyMilestones: At least one software systems design question
Two or three behavioural questions per interviewer, mapped to assigned Leadership Principles
Bar Raiser interview by a trained interviewer from another team
checklistItems: Prepare enough distinct stories that you never reuse one across interviewers - they compare notes in the debrief
Rehearse the six design objectives Amazon names: practicality, accuracy, efficiency, reliability, optimization, scalability
Bring metrics. Amazon tells candidates to include data because it is a data-driven company

roadmapStages.title: Debrief and offer
roadmapStages.description: Interviewers write up feedback, the Bar Raiser and hiring manager drive the decision, and a Business Partner or Recruiter contacts you with the outcome, compensation and onboarding.
keyMilestones: Bar Raiser and hiring manager make the final call
Business Partner or Recruiter handles offer, compensation, visa and onboarding
checklistItems: Ask your recruiter about compensation philosophy - Amazon directs that question to the recruiter
Allow two business days for recruiter replies; Amazon states this repeatedly
Complete both post-interview surveys - they differ by stage

rounds.name: Online Assessment

structureClaim.value: Four sections with published average times. Since January 2026 the coding section places candidates on a real coding platform alongside an interactive AI assistant.
structureClaim.quote: work with an interactive AI assistant on a real coding platform

rounds.focusSummary: Algorithmic correctness under time pressure, plus two separate Leadership Principles instruments that most candidates underestimate.

whatTheyLookFor: All hidden test cases passing, including boundary and empty inputs
Complexity that survives large inputs rather than the first working idea
greenFlags: Optimal or near-optimal complexity on both problems
Clean helper decomposition rather than one long function
redFlags: Time-limit exceeded from a quadratic scan over a large input
Hard-coded handling of the sample cases

whatTheyLookFor: Answers that consistently pick customer impact and ownership over convenience
The same behavioural profile across both instruments
greenFlags: Decisive choices that name a customer consequence
Willingness to escalate or dive into detail rather than defer
redFlags: Neutral, middle-of-the-road answers throughout
A Workstyles profile that contradicts the Work Simulation choices

sampleQuestions.title: Optimal scheduling over a large input
sampleQuestions.prompt: Given up to 10^5 intervals, select the maximum number that do not overlap. Amazon lists algorithms and data structures as core interview topics and the OA is time-boxed, so comparing every pair will not finish.
keyPointsToCover: Sort by end time, then sweep once
State the O(n log n) bound before you write it
Handle touching intervals explicitly - the boundary case is the hidden test

provenance.value: Amazon lists "Data structures" and "Algorithms" among the topics it assesses for software development roles.

sampleQuestions.title: Workstyles: the missed dependency
sampleQuestions.prompt: A dependency you own will slip and break a partner team launch. Rank the actions you would take first.
keyPointsToCover: Tell the partner team immediately rather than after you have a fix
Own the slip without distributing blame
Offer a concrete mitigation and a date

provenance.value: Amazon publishes that the OA contains a Workstyles Assessment and a Work Simulation alongside the coding section.

insiderTips.value: Practise without an IDE. Amazon recommends this explicitly.
Do not screenshot. Amazon terminates the session.

rounds.name: Phone screen

structureClaim.value: One or two phone interviews conducted over Amazon Chime or Zoom, which may be followed by role-specific assessments.
structureClaim.quote: one or two phone interviews via Amazon Chime / Zoom

rounds.interviewerRole: Amazon SDE, usually from the hiring team
rounds.focusSummary: A single coding problem in a shared editor plus the first Leadership Principles probes. Amazon says phone screens often assess basic qualifications.

whatTheyLookFor: Clarifying questions before code
A stated brute force, then a stated optimisation
greenFlags: Narrates the trade-off before choosing
Tests the code against an edge case unprompted
redFlags: Silent typing
Jumps to an optimal solution with no explanation of why

whatTheyLookFor: STAR structure with a real result
Metrics attached to the result
greenFlags: Names what they personally did, not what the team did
redFlags: We instead of I throughout the story

sampleQuestions.title: Tell me about a time you had to dive deep into a problem others had given up on
sampleQuestions.prompt: Amazon states that interviewers ask two or three behavioural questions each, drawn from the Leadership Principles, and that past behaviour is an indicator of future success.
keyPointsToCover: The specific signal you noticed that others had dismissed
The investigative steps, in order
The measured outcome

provenance.value: Amazon publishes Dive Deep as one of its 16 Leadership Principles and says interviewers ask two or three behavioural questions each.
provenance.quote: Each interviewer will typically ask two or three behavioral-based questions

insiderTips.value: Amazon publishes a decision SLA of two business days after the phone screen. If you hear nothing, your recruiter is the named contact.
Interview transcription is voluntary and your choice does not affect evaluation. You can also withdraw consent mid-interview.
insiderTips.quote: Interview transcription is voluntary, and your choice will not affect how your application is evaluated.

rounds.name: Loop: coding and data structures

structureClaim.value: The SDE II loop is four 55-minute interviews. Every interviewer covers both technical competencies and assigned Leadership Principles.
structureClaim.quote: both technical competencies and non-technical competencies that are based off of our Leadership Principles, which different interviewers will be assigned to evaluate

rounds.interviewerRole: SDE II or Senior SDE from the hiring org
rounds.focusSummary: Data structures and algorithms under discussion, with roughly a third of the slot reserved for Leadership Principles.

whatTheyLookFor: Correct choice of structure for the access pattern
Working code, then optimisation
Edge cases named before they are hit
greenFlags: Reaches for the right structure without prompting
Self-corrects after dry running
redFlags: Cannot state the complexity of their own solution
Needs the interviewer to supply the approach

whatTheyLookFor: Two or three STAR stories with data
Ownership language
greenFlags: Different stories from the ones given to other interviewers
redFlags: Reused story the debrief has already heard

sampleQuestions.title: Design a data structure with O(1) insert, delete and getRandom
sampleQuestions.prompt: Support insert, remove and getRandom in average constant time. Amazon lists data structures and object-oriented design among its published interview topics.
keyPointsToCover: Array for O(1) random access plus a map from value to index
Swap-with-last on delete to keep the array dense
What happens on duplicate inserts - ask before you assume

provenance.value: Amazon lists "Data structures", "Algorithms" and "Object-oriented design" among its published software development interview topics.

sampleQuestions.title: Word ladder over a large dictionary
sampleQuestions.prompt: Find the shortest transformation sequence between two words. This is the canonical test of whether you model a problem as a graph unprompted.
keyPointsToCover: Recognise it as unweighted shortest path, so BFS not DFS
Build the wildcard bucket index instead of comparing every pair
Bidirectional BFS as the optimisation to mention

provenance.value: Amazon lists "Algorithms" among its published interview topics.

insiderTips.value: Amazon states it will not ask brain teasers.
You may share your screen to show work, but only content relevant to the question and never personal data.

rounds.name: Loop: software systems design

structureClaim.value: Amazon tells SDE II candidates to expect at least one question on software systems design, and publishes the six objectives it scores the design against.
structureClaim.quote: expect at least one question on software systems design

rounds.focusSummary: Amazon publishes the exact six objectives: practicality, accuracy, efficiency, reliability, optimization, scalability. Use them as your own agenda.

whatTheyLookFor: A design that could actually be built by a team this quarter
greenFlags: Chooses a boring, operable component over a clever one
redFlags: Invents infrastructure that does not exist

whatTheyLookFor: The design solves the stated requirement, not an adjacent one
greenFlags: Restates requirements and gets them confirmed
redFlags: Designs the system they rehearsed rather than the one asked for

whatTheyLookFor: Sensible cost and latency reasoning
greenFlags: Estimates traffic and storage before choosing components
redFlags: No numbers anywhere in the design

whatTheyLookFor: Failure modes named and handled
greenFlags: Talks about what happens when a dependency is down
redFlags: Assumes every call succeeds

whatTheyLookFor: Knows which bottleneck matters and attacks that one
greenFlags: Identifies the hot path before optimising
redFlags: Micro-optimises a component that is not the constraint

whatTheyLookFor: A clear story for 10x growth
greenFlags: Partitioning strategy with a named partition key
redFlags: Just add more servers, with no data story

sampleQuestions.title: Design a globally replicated key-value store with tunable consistency
sampleQuestions.prompt: Amazon lists distributed computing as a published interview topic, and its own Builders Library documents the operational patterns it expects engineers to know.
keyPointsToCover: Consistent hashing and the partition key choice
Quorum reads and writes; what R + W > N buys you
Conflict resolution and why last-writer-wins is a product decision
Walk the six objectives explicitly - Amazon publishes them

provenance.value: Amazon lists "Distributed computing" as a published interview topic and publishes the six design objectives it scores against.

insiderTips.value: Amazon says you should ask questions to complete and validate your design. Treat the first five minutes as requirement gathering, not architecture.
insiderTips.quote: should ask questions to complete and validate your design

rounds.name: Bar Raiser

structureClaim.value: A specially trained interviewer from outside the hiring team joins the loop as an objective third party and is a steward of the 16 Leadership Principles. Amazon says there are more than 3,600 Bar Raisers.
structureClaim.quote: a specially trained interviewer who ensures our hiring standards remain consistently high across all teams

rounds.interviewerRole: Trained Bar Raiser from an unrelated organisation
rounds.focusSummary: Whether you raise the bar, which Amazon defines as being better than 50 percent of people currently in similar roles.

whatTheyLookFor: Evidence you are stronger than the median incumbent at this level
Long-term potential, not just fit for this one team
greenFlags: Stories that show growth in scope over time
Candid account of a real failure and what changed
redFlags: Every story is a success
Cannot articulate what they would do differently

whatTheyLookFor: Fresh stories, since the Bar Raiser sees the whole loop written feedback
greenFlags: Specific detail that survives follow-up probing
redFlags: Detail evaporates when the interviewer digs in

sampleQuestions.title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager and had to commit anyway
sampleQuestions.prompt: Amazon publishes this principle as: leaders are obligated to respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when doing so is uncomfortable.
keyPointsToCover: The substance of the disagreement, not the feeling
How you escalated and what evidence you brought
That you genuinely committed afterwards - the commit half is the test

provenance.value: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit is one of the 16 published Leadership Principles.

insiderTips.value: Bar Raisers are nominated by peers and trained for three months to a year, shadowing veteran Bar Raisers. They do this on top of their real job.
Bar Raisers are widely described as holding a veto over the hire. Amazon itself only says the Bar Raiser drives the decision alongside the hiring manager - it publishes no formal veto.
insiderTips.note: This is the single most-repeated claim about Amazon hiring that the company does not confirm in writing. Treat it as a strong norm, not a documented rule.

behavioralRubric.philosophyTitle: The 16 Leadership Principles

description.value: Every Amazon interviewer is assigned specific Leadership Principles to evaluate, and typically asks two or three behavioural questions each. Amazon tells candidates to use the STAR method and to bring metrics.
description.quote: Each interviewer will typically ask two or three behavioral-based questions about successes or challenges and how you handled them using our Leadership Principles.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders start with the customer and work backwards. They work vigorously to earn and keep customer trust.
officialDefinition.quote: Leaders start with the customer and work backwards. They work vigorously to earn and keep customer trust.

principles.meaning: Decisions begin from the customer consequence, not the engineering convenience. Internal customers count.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you went significantly beyond what was asked for a customer.
Describe a time you pushed back on a requirement because it was wrong for the customer.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Open with the customer signal - a ticket, a metric, a complaint. Make the result a customer number, not a delivery date.
principles.commonPitfalls: Telling a story where the customer is invisible and the win is purely technical.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders are owners. They think long term and do not sacrifice long-term value for short-term results.

principles.meaning: You never say that is not my job. You pick up the thing nobody owns.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you took on something outside your responsibilities.
Describe a time you had to fix something you did not break.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Show the moment you chose to own it, and the long-term cost you avoided.
principles.commonPitfalls: Framing it as heroics rather than judgement.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders expect and require innovation and invention from their teams and always find ways to simplify.

principles.meaning: The simplification half is scored as heavily as the invention half.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about the most complex thing you made simple.
Describe an invention of yours that someone else adopted.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Quantify the removed complexity - lines deleted, services collapsed, steps removed.
principles.commonPitfalls: Describing a novel system that made the codebase harder to operate.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders have strong judgment and good instincts. They seek diverse perspectives and work to disconfirm their beliefs.

principles.meaning: The disconfirming half is the interesting half. Show you went looking for evidence you were wrong.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a judgement call you made with incomplete data.
Describe a time you changed your mind because of someone else data.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Name the belief, the disconfirming test you ran, and what you did with the answer.
principles.commonPitfalls: A story where you were simply right and everyone agreed.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders are never done learning and always seek to improve themselves. They are curious about new possibilities and act to explore them.

principles.meaning: Learning that produced an action, not learning as a hobby.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about something you taught yourself that changed how you work.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Connect the learning to a shipped outcome.
principles.commonPitfalls: Listing courses with no downstream effect.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders raise the performance bar with every hire and promotion. They recognize exceptional talent, and willingly move them throughout the organization.

principles.meaning: Even at SDE I this shows up as mentoring, onboarding and raising code-review standards.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about someone you helped get better.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Make the other person the protagonist and show their measurable improvement.
principles.commonPitfalls: Claiming credit for their growth.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders have relentlessly high standards - many people may think these standards are unreasonably high.

principles.meaning: Refusing to ship something you know is below bar, and the cost you paid for that.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you refused to ship.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Quantify the defect you prevented.
principles.commonPitfalls: Perfectionism with no delivery.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders create and communicate a bold direction that inspires results. They think differently and look around corners.

principles.meaning: Scope beyond your ticket. What would this look like for every team, not just yours?
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you proposed something much larger than you were asked for.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Show that the bold direction was adopted by someone with authority.
principles.commonPitfalls: A grand idea that never left your head.

officialDefinition.value: Speed matters in business. Many decisions and actions are reversible and do not need extensive study.
officialDefinition.quote: Speed matters in business. Many decisions and actions are reversible and do not need extensive study.

principles.meaning: Distinguish the reversible decision you made fast from the irreversible one you studied.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a decision you made without full information.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Name explicitly why the decision was reversible.
principles.commonPitfalls: Recklessness dressed up as speed.

officialDefinition.value: Accomplish more with less. Constraints breed resourcefulness, self-sufficiency and invention.
officialDefinition.quote: Accomplish more with less. Constraints breed resourcefulness, self-sufficiency and invention.

principles.meaning: Cost awareness is engineering signal: cloud spend, headcount, build vs buy.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you delivered with far fewer resources than you wanted.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Put a currency figure or a percentage on what you saved.
principles.commonPitfalls: Cutting corners and calling it frugality.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders listen attentively, speak candidly, and treat others respectfully. They are vocally self-critical.
officialDefinition.quote: Leaders listen attentively, speak candidly, and treat others respectfully. They are vocally self-critical.

principles.meaning: Vocally self-critical is the phrase to take literally. Have a real failure ready.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about your biggest professional mistake.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Own it without hedging, then show the systemic change you made.
principles.commonPitfalls: A humblebrag failure such as caring too much.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, audit frequently, and are skeptical when metrics differ.

principles.meaning: Root cause, not symptom. Expect the interviewer to keep asking why.
sampleQuestions: Walk me through the hardest bug you have debugged.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Go three levels deeper than feels necessary. The probing is the test.
principles.commonPitfalls: Detail that evaporates under follow-up.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders are obligated to respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when uncomfortable.

principles.meaning: Both halves are scored. Disagreeing and then sulking fails.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Spend as much time on how you committed as on how you disagreed.
principles.commonPitfalls: Stories where you were vindicated and never had to commit.

officialDefinition.value: Leaders focus on the key inputs for their business and deliver them with the right quality and timeliness.

principles.meaning: The default close for any story. Land the number.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a deadline you thought you would miss.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Inputs you controlled, then the output metric.
principles.commonPitfalls: Effort without outcome.

principles.principle: Strive to be Earth’s Best Employer

officialDefinition.value: Leaders work every day to create a safer, more productive, higher performing, more diverse work environment.

principles.meaning: Rarely the headline question, but a good fallback for team-health stories.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about something you changed to make your team work better.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Show adoption by the team, not just your intent.
principles.commonPitfalls: Generic culture talk.

principles.principle: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility

officialDefinition.value: We are big, we impact the world, and we are far from perfect. We must be humble and thoughtful about the effects of our actions.

principles.meaning: Second-order consequences: privacy, safety, sustainability, abuse vectors.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you considered the downstream harm of something you built.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Name the harm you anticipated and the mitigation you shipped.
principles.commonPitfalls: Treating it as a corporate-social-responsibility question.

qaBank.question: How long is the Amazon SDE online assessment, and what is actually in it?

provenance.value: Amazon publishes the section-by-section breakdown on its university SDE page.

answer.approach: Budget two hours for a full-time SDE OA and about 90 minutes for an internship OA. They are not the same assessment.
keyPoints: Full-time: Coding (avg 70 min), Workstyles (avg 15 min), Work Simulation (avg 60 min), Feedback Survey (avg 5 min)
Internship: Coding, Workstyles, Feedback Survey - no Work Simulation
The times Amazon publishes are averages, not hard caps
Two of the four sections are behavioural, which is where most candidates under-prepare
pitfalls: Preparing only the algorithms and walking into the Work Simulation cold
Using print screen, which terminates the session
Copying and pasting inside the assessment, which Amazon tells you to avoid
followUps: Is there a published passing score? No - Amazon publishes no cutoff.
Which platform? Amazon points at a HackerRank sample challenge.

qaBank.question: What exactly does the Bar Raiser do, and can they veto my offer?

provenance.value: Amazon publishes a dedicated explainer on the Bar Raiser programme.

answer.approach: Separate what Amazon states from what the internet repeats. Amazon states the role, the training and the standard. It does not state a veto.
keyPoints: The Bar Raiser is an objective third party from outside the hiring team
They are nominated by managers, peers or other Bar Raisers and train for three months to a year
They are a steward of the 16 Leadership Principles
Amazon says there are more than 3,600 Bar Raisers, doing it on top of their normal job
The published standard: the candidate should be better than 50 percent of people currently in similar roles
pitfalls: Assuming the Bar Raiser round is softer because they are not on the team - it is usually the deepest probing
Reusing a story another interviewer already heard; the Bar Raiser reads the whole loop written feedback
followUps: Do they have a formal veto? Amazon does not say so. The company describes the decision as made with the hiring manager.
Can you tell who the Bar Raiser is? Not reliably, and it should not change how you answer.

practiceLinks.label: About Amazon: What is an Amazon Bar Raiser?

qaBank.question: How should I structure a system design answer at Amazon specifically?

provenance.value: Amazon publishes the six objectives it evaluates system design against on its SDE II prep page.

answer.approach: Use the six objectives Amazon publishes as your spoken agenda. Very few candidates do this, and it maps your answer straight onto the scoring sheet.
keyPoints: Practicality - could a real team build and operate this
Accuracy - does it solve the requirement you were actually given
Efficiency - cost and latency reasoning with numbers
Reliability - what happens when each dependency fails
Optimization - which bottleneck actually matters
Scalability - the 10x story, with a named partition key
Amazon also says to ask questions to complete and validate your design
answer.complexity: Spend the first 10 minutes on requirements. A design that is accurate against the wrong requirement scores zero on accuracy.
pitfalls: Designing the system you rehearsed rather than the one you were asked for
No traffic or storage estimates anywhere
Treating scalability as add more servers with no data partitioning story
followUps: How deep should the deep dive go? One component, properly, beats five sketched.
Do they expect specific AWS services? Naming them helps but the reasoning is what is scored.

qaBank.question: When will I actually hear back from Amazon?

provenance.value: Amazon publishes a decision SLA in its interview FAQ and in its newsroom.

answer.approach: Amazon is one of the very few companies that publishes a response deadline. Hold them to it.
keyPoints: Within two business days after your phone interview
Within five business days after your interview loop
The process as a whole averages three to six weeks
If you pass those windows, your recruiter is the named escalation contact
Allow two business days for a recruiter to reply to you
pitfalls: Chasing on day one after the loop
Emailing the scheduler about the outcome - the Business Partner or Recruiter owns that conversation
followUps: Who handles compensation questions? The Business Partner or Recruiter.
What if the role closes after you pass? Amazon keeps your interview record on file and may route you to a similar role.

qaBank.question: Should I accept AI interview transcription?

provenance.value: Amazon documents the transcription feature, its access controls and its opt-out in its FAQ.

answer.approach: It is genuinely voluntary and Amazon states the choice does not affect evaluation. Decide on the access model, not on nerves.
keyPoints: It records and transcribes the conversation so interviewers can stop taking notes
Access is limited to your loop interviewers, the Bar Raiser and the hiring manager
Transcripts cannot be downloaded or shared outside the evaluation system
You will not receive a copy - transcripts are internal evaluation material
You can decline in your profile, or withdraw consent mid-interview by telling the interviewer
Amazon reports 83% of candidates found interactions more engaging with it on
pitfalls: Assuming declining counts against you - Amazon states explicitly that it does not
Forgetting to update your profile after withdrawing consent, so the preference does not carry to later interviews
followUps: Does it apply to the OA? The transcription feature is described for interviews, not the assessment.

evaluationFramework.name: Bar Raiser and hiring manager debrief

howItWorks.value: Interviewers are each assigned specific Leadership Principles, write up structured feedback, and meet in a debrief. A trained Bar Raiser from outside the team joins the loop as an objective third party and is a steward of the Leadership Principles.

blockingAuthority.value: The Bar Raiser is widely understood to be able to block a hire. Amazon itself describes the Bar Raiser as driving the decision together with the hiring manager and publishes no formal veto.
blockingAuthority.note: Flagged deliberately: this is the most repeated unverified claim about Amazon hiring.

offerDecisionMaker.value: A Business Partner or Recruiter contacts you with the outcome and next steps, and owns compensation, visa and onboarding conversations.

recentChanges.value: January 2026: Amazon put an interactive AI assistant into the technical assessment on a real coding platform, reporting that 87% of candidates felt the questions related to the role they were pursuing.
AI interview transcription rolled out with explicit consent required, and Amazon reports 83% of candidates found interactions more engaging.
Machine-learning job matching replaced keyword matching; Amazon reports candidates matched this way who reach interview are 24% more likely to receive a positive outcome.
General machine learning and artificial intelligence now appears on the published SDE interview topic list alongside the classic CS fundamentals.

companies.name: Google
companies.tagline: Publishes a hiring philosophy and interview tips, but almost nothing about its actual loop mechanics. Most of what candidates repeat about Google hiring is community knowledge, not company statement - and this page says which is which.
companies.transparencyNote: Honest warning: Google publishes far less about its interview process than its reputation suggests. Its careers pages cover resume advice and interview tips, and its site does not expose the round structure, the rubric names, or how the hiring committee works. Everything on this page about GCA, RRK, Googleyness, the hiring committee and level mapping is labelled reported, because Google does not state it on a page we can cite. We would rather tell you that than invent a rubric.

sources.label: Interviewing at Google: best practices, advice, and tips

hiringPhilosophy.value: Google frames its process around giving every candidate, from entry level to leadership, access to the same information and resources.
hiringPhilosophy.quote: We want all candidates - from entry-level to leadership - to have access to the same information and resources

levels.title: Software Engineer II (new grad)
levels.primaryExpectation: Strong CS fundamentals, clean code, and the ability to explain your reasoning as you go.

levels.title: Software Engineer III
levels.primaryExpectation: Own a component; hold a system design conversation; show measurable impact.

levels.title: Senior Software Engineer
levels.primaryExpectation: Technical leadership across teams, and design depth that survives adversarial questioning.

totalRounds.value: Commonly reported as a recruiter screen, one or two technical phone screens, and a four-to-five interview onsite, followed by committee review and team matching.
totalRounds.note: Google does not publish its round count or loop composition. This reflects widely repeated candidate accounts, not a company statement.

averageHiringTimeline.value: Frequently reported as six weeks to several months, heavily dependent on team matching.
averageHiringTimeline.note: Google publishes no timeline. Unlike Amazon and Meta, there is no company-stated duration to cite.

platformClaim.value: Google does not publish a standard online assessment for experienced software engineering hires.
platformClaim.note: Some university and early-career pipelines have used a sample coding assessment, but Google publishes no standing OA specification, so we do not list one.

sectionsClaim.value: No company-published assessment structure exists to describe.
sectionsClaim.note: Deliberately left empty rather than filled with invented section timings.

tips.value: Cross-reference your resume against the job description and build a library of examples you can draw on during the interview.
tips.quote: Cross-reference your resume with the job description to help you connect the dots between the two. Where there's overlap, build out a library of examples that you can draw from during the interview

tips.value: Expect questions phrased as tell me about a time when, or how would you approach this situation.
tips.quote: Many of the questions we ask will be along the lines of "Tell me about a time when..." or "How would you approach this situation...?"

tips.value: Use data to illustrate impact. Google states plainly that it loves data and wants to see achievements quantified.
tips.quote: Google loves data, and we especially love to see how you use data to illustrate how your achievements have made an impact

tips.value: Build the resume for the job, not the job for the resume: Google advises starting from a blank document for each role.
tips.quote: start with a blank document and build a resume specifically designed for each job you want

roadmapStages.title: Resume and application
roadmapStages.description: Google publishes explicit resume guidance and tells candidates to build a fresh resume per role rather than reusing an old one.
checklistItems: Start from a blank document for each role - Google says this directly
Quantify impact; Google states it loves data
Cross-reference the job description and build an example library before you interview

roadmapStages.title: Recruiter screen
roadmapStages.description: Background, motivation, level calibration and logistics.
checklistItems: Have your example library ready before this call
Ask which interview types your loop contains

roadmapStages.title: Technical phone screen
roadmapStages.description: One or two technical conversations with a Google engineer. Google publishes no specification for this stage.
keyMilestones: Live coding in a shared document or editor
checklistItems: Practise coding in a plain shared doc with no autocomplete
State complexity before you are asked

roadmapStages.title: Onsite loop
roadmapStages.description: Multiple back-to-back technical interviews plus a behavioural conversation. Composition is not published by Google.
keyMilestones: System design for mid and senior levels
checklistItems: Prepare to narrate continuously - Google emphasises thought process in its published tips
Have quantified stories ready; Google asks tell-me-about-a-time questions

roadmapStages.title: Committee review and team matching
roadmapStages.description: Widely reported as a packet review by a committee that did not interview you, followed by team matching. Google does not describe this publicly.
checklistItems: Ask your recruiter directly what stage you are at - the committee stage is invisible from outside
Keep interviewing elsewhere; team matching can add weeks

rounds.name: Technical phone screen

structureClaim.value: A live coding conversation with a Google engineer, typically 45 minutes, usually in a shared document.
structureClaim.note: Google publishes no round specification. This is the consistently reported format.

rounds.focusSummary: Data structures and algorithms with continuous narration of your reasoning.

whatTheyLookFor: A stated approach before code
Correct complexity reasoning
greenFlags: Considers more than one approach and picks with a reason
redFlags: Silence, or code first and think later

whatTheyLookFor: Compilable, readable code without an IDE
greenFlags: Names variables well under pressure
Dry runs the code
redFlags: Pseudo-code where real code was asked for

sampleQuestions.title: Design and implement an LRU cache
sampleQuestions.prompt: Constant-time get and put. The classic test of whether you can combine a hash map and a doubly linked list correctly under time pressure.
keyPointsToCover: Hash map to node pointers plus a doubly linked list for recency
Eviction on capacity, and updating recency on get as well as put
Sentinel head and tail nodes to avoid null checks

provenance.value: A staple of reported Google phone screens. Google does not publish sample questions for this stage.

insiderTips.value: Google publishes that many of its questions take the form tell me about a time when, even inside technical loops. Have quantified examples ready.

rounds.name: Onsite coding

structureClaim.value: Two to three coding interviews in the onsite loop, each around 45 minutes.
structureClaim.note: Loop composition is not published by Google.

rounds.interviewerRole: Google software engineer, often outside the hiring team
rounds.focusSummary: Algorithmic depth plus the quality of the conversation around it.

whatTheyLookFor: Optimal or near-optimal solution reached through reasoning
greenFlags: Identifies the underlying pattern quickly and says which one
redFlags: Pattern matched to a memorised solution that does not fit

whatTheyLookFor: Continuous, structured narration
greenFlags: Checks in with the interviewer before committing to an approach
redFlags: Long silences

sampleQuestions.title: Word search on a grid with a dictionary
sampleQuestions.prompt: Find all dictionary words present in a character grid. The naive search per word is far too slow.
keyPointsToCover: Build a trie from the dictionary and walk the grid once
Prune dead branches as soon as the prefix leaves the trie
Mark and restore visited cells correctly

provenance.value: A commonly reported Google onsite problem shape.

insiderTips.value: Google publishes the Tech Dev Guide as its own free preparation curriculum. It is the closest thing to an official syllabus the company offers.

rounds.name: System design

structureClaim.value: One system design interview for mid-level and above.

rounds.focusSummary: Designing something planet-scale without losing the thread on failure modes.

whatTheyLookFor: Requirements and scale estimated before components
greenFlags: Back-of-envelope numbers driving the design
redFlags: No numbers anywhere

whatTheyLookFor: One component explored properly
greenFlags: Storage layout and index choice justified
redFlags: Breadth with no depth

sampleQuestions.title: Design a web-scale crawler and index
sampleQuestions.prompt: Crawl politely at scale, deduplicate, and build an index that answers queries in milliseconds. Google publishes extensive research on the underlying systems problems.
keyPointsToCover: Frontier management and politeness per host
Content deduplication, for example with shingling
Inverted index construction and sharding strategy
Freshness vs cost of recrawling

provenance.value: Google publishes its systems research openly, which is the most defensible grounding for what it considers interesting design territory.

insiderTips.value: Ask the interviewer to confirm the scale you should design for before you commit.
insiderTips.note: General good practice; not a Google-published instruction.

rounds.name: Behavioural conversation

structureClaim.value: Google publishes that many of its questions follow the tell-me-about-a-time and how-would-you-approach patterns, and that it wants data attached to achievements.

rounds.focusSummary: How you work with others, handle ambiguity, and evidence impact with data.

whatTheyLookFor: Achievements expressed as measured outcomes
greenFlags: A number with a baseline and a timeframe
redFlags: Adjectives instead of metrics

whatTheyLookFor: Working without clear direction
Handling disagreement
greenFlags: Names what someone else contributed
redFlags: Sole-hero narration

sampleQuestions.title: Tell me about a time you had to make progress without clear direction
sampleQuestions.prompt: Google publishes that its questions commonly take the tell-me-about-a-time form, and that it wants to see data illustrating impact.
keyPointsToCover: What was ambiguous, specifically
How you narrowed it down
The measured result, with a baseline

provenance.value: Google publishes both the question shape and the data expectation.

insiderTips.value: Build the example library before the loop, not during it. Google recommends exactly this on its interview tips page.

rationale.value: The most consistently reported Google interview category across candidate accounts. Google publishes no topic list.

typicalPatterns: BFS and DFS on implicit graphs
Tree recursion with a return contract

rationale.value: Heavily reported at Google relative to other FAANG loops.
Search-adjacent problems appear often in reported Google loops.
Google publishes its own Tech Dev Guide covering algorithmic foundations as its recommended preparation path.

typicalPatterns: Choosing the bound that matters in practice

systemDesignTopics.title: Web-scale crawler and inverted index
systemDesignTopics.description: Crawl, deduplicate, index, serve - the design that maps most directly onto Google research output.
keyTradeoffsToDiscuss: Index sharding by document vs by term
Tail latency in the serving tier

grounding.value: Google publishes its systems research openly at research.google.

systemDesignTopics.title: Globally consistent transactional datastore
systemDesignTopics.description: External consistency across regions and what it costs in latency.

grounding.value: Google publishes its distributed-systems research openly.

systemDesignTopics.title: Large-scale batch and stream processing pipeline
systemDesignTopics.description: Windowing, watermarks, and what correctness means when events arrive late.

grounding.value: Google publishes its dataflow and stream-processing research openly.

behavioralRubric.philosophyTitle: What Google actually publishes about behavioural interviews

description.value: Google publishes the question shapes it uses and the expectation that achievements come with data. It does not publish a named behavioural rubric.

officialDefinition.value: Google loves data, and especially loves seeing how you use data to illustrate the impact of your achievements.
officialDefinition.quote: Google loves data, and we especially love to see how you use data to illustrate how your achievements have made an impact

principles.meaning: Every story should land on a number with a baseline and a timeframe.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about your highest-impact project. How did you measure the impact?
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Baseline, intervention, measured delta, timeframe. In that order.
principles.commonPitfalls: Impressive-sounding scope with no measurement.

officialDefinition.value: Many questions take the form tell me about a time when, or how would you approach this situation.
officialDefinition.quote: Many of the questions we ask will be along the lines of "Tell me about a time when..." or "How would you approach this situation...?"

principles.meaning: Half the behavioural questions are hypothetical rather than historical. Prepare both modes.
sampleQuestions: How would you approach a project where two senior engineers disagree on the architecture?
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: For hypotheticals, state your information-gathering step first, then your decision criteria, then the decision.
principles.commonPitfalls: Answering a hypothetical with a past anecdote that does not actually fit.

officialDefinition.value: Cross-reference your resume with the job description and build a library of examples to draw from.

principles.meaning: Google is telling you the preparation method it wants. Very few candidates follow it literally.
sampleQuestions: Walk me through how your background maps to this role.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Have three examples per requirement line in the job description.
principles.commonPitfalls: One general story reused for every question.

principles.meaning: The four-attribute framework - general cognitive ability, role-related knowledge, leadership, Googleyness - is what candidates and coaches describe. Google does not publish it on a page we can cite.
sampleQuestions: Tell me about a time you worked with someone very different from you.
Describe a problem you solved that had no precedent.
principles.starAnsweringStrategy: Treat it as ordinary behavioural preparation. Do not optimise for a rubric that the company has not published.
principles.commonPitfalls: Contorting answers to fit a four-attribute framework that no Google page confirms. Prepare substance, not vocabulary.

summary.value: Google publishes its systems research and its own developer preparation curriculum, which together are the most defensible picture of what it builds and what it expects you to know.

backendAndServices.name: gRPC and Protocol Buffers
backendAndServices.note: Both originated at Google and are published openly.

whatTheyActuallyTest.value: Quantified impact - Google states it wants data illustrating achievements.
Situational and behavioural reasoning in both past and hypothetical form.
Algorithmic depth, especially graphs, dynamic programming and complexity reasoning.
whatTheyActuallyTest.note: Google publishes the Tech Dev Guide curriculum but not an interview topic list.

headline.value: Google has no candidate-facing AI interview policy that we could find on its own careers site.
headline.note: Press outlets have reported on Google piloting AI-assisted coding interviews, but we do not treat press reports of an unreleased pilot as policy. Ask your recruiter what applies to your specific loop - that is the only reliable answer today.

allowed.value: Using AI to research the company and the role before you interview is unremarkable; Google publishes no restriction on preparation.
allowed.quote: Cross-reference your resume with the job description

prohibited.value: Assume live-interview AI use is not permitted unless your recruiter tells you otherwise.
prohibited.note: Google publishes no rule either way. This is the conservative default, not a company statement.

qaBank.question: Is the GCA / RRK / Leadership / Googleyness rubric real?

provenance.value: The four-attribute framework is described by interview coaching sites and ex-Googlers, not on a Google careers page we can cite.
provenance.note: We searched Google own careers pages and could not find it published.

answer.approach: Treat it as folklore that is probably directionally right but is not something Google publishes. Prepare substance rather than vocabulary.
keyPoints: Google publishes interview tips and resume guidance, not a named rubric
What Google does publish: question shapes, and the expectation that impact comes with data
Coaching sites present the four attributes with confidence; none of them cite a Google page
Answering in the language of a rubric the interviewer is not using looks rehearsed
pitfalls: Labelling your own answers as demonstrating Googleyness out loud
Skipping ordinary preparation because you optimised for a framework
followUps: What should I prepare instead? Quantified stories, both historical and hypothetical, per the published tips.
Should I ask my recruiter? Yes - they will tell you which interview types are in your loop.

qaBank.question: What does Google actually tell candidates to do?

provenance.value: Taken directly from Google own interview tips and hiring process pages.

answer.approach: Four concrete instructions, all in Google own words. They are more actionable than most rubric speculation.
keyPoints: Cross-reference your resume with the job description and build a library of examples
Practise delivering those examples out loud before interview day
Expect tell-me-about-a-time and how-would-you-approach questions
Use data to illustrate the impact of your achievements
Start each resume from a blank document, designed for that specific job
pitfalls: Reusing a single generic resume across every Google application
Preparing only algorithms and treating the behavioural round as a formality
followUps: Where is the official prep curriculum? Google Tech Dev Guide.

qaBank.question: Can I use AI in a Google interview?

provenance.value: No Google careers page states a candidate AI policy.
provenance.note: Compare with Meta, which publishes an explicit expectation, and Snowflake and Datadog, which publish explicit restrictions.

answer.approach: Ask your recruiter. Do not infer a policy from press coverage of a pilot.
keyPoints: Google publishes no candidate-facing AI interview policy that we could locate
Press outlets have reported on an AI-assisted coding interview pilot; a pilot is not a published policy
The safe default is to assume no AI in live rounds unless told otherwise
Using AI to prepare is uncontroversial everywhere, including here
pitfalls: Reading a news headline and assuming it applies to your loop
Opening an AI tool mid-interview without explicit permission
followUps: Who has published a policy? Meta expects AI use; Snowflake and Datadog restrict it; Amazon builds it into the assessment.

evaluationFramework.name: Hiring committee review (reported)

howItWorks.value: Interviewer feedback is compiled into a packet and reviewed by a committee of Googlers who did not interview you, followed by team matching. Google does not describe this on a page we can cite.
howItWorks.note: Flagged: this is the best-known fact about Google hiring and also one of the least officially documented.

blockingAuthority.value: The committee, rather than the hiring manager, is reported to make the hire recommendation.

offerDecisionMaker.value: Your recruiter is the only reliable source of truth on where your packet is.
offerDecisionMaker.note: Google publishes no description of the decision chain.

recentChanges.value: Press outlets reported through 2026 that Google was piloting AI-assisted coding interviews for software engineers.
recentChanges.note: Reported by news outlets rather than announced by Google on its careers site. We have deliberately not promoted this to a verified claim.

recentChanges.value: Google continues to publish the Tech Dev Guide as its own free preparation curriculum, which remains the most official prep resource it offers.

companies.name: Meta
companies.tagline: The first major employer to make AI use mandatory in its coding interview. Meta now expects you to work with an AI assistant inside CoderPad and scores you on how well you do it.
companies.transparencyNote: Meta rewrote its published interview FAQ in 2026 to describe AI-native technical interviews, and the detail there is unusually specific: which models are available, which languages are supported, and how design interviews are now run. What Meta still does not publish is the internal round-by-round loop composition or the level-by-level rubric, so anything at that granularity here is labelled as reported.

companies.transparencyNote: We searched apple.com and jobs.apple.com and found no published interview-process or interview-preparation page for software engineering roles. That is itself the most useful fact about interviewing at Apple: there is no company-stated loop, no published rubric, no stated timeline and no AI policy. Everything below except the job-listing detail is community-reported, and we have deliberately kept this profile shorter than the others rather than padding it with confident-sounding invention.

sampleQuestions.title: Match riders to nearby drivers efficiently
sampleQuestions.prompt: Given a stream of driver location updates and a rider request, return the nearest available drivers quickly. Uber uses real-world problems rather than puzzles, and this is as real-world as it gets for them.
keyPointsToCover: Spatial partitioning - a grid or hierarchical hex index rather than scanning all drivers
Handling the write volume of continuous location updates
Road distance versus straight-line distance, and when the approximation is acceptable
State the complexity of both the update and the query path

provenance.value: Uber states its interviewers use real-world problems, not logic puzzles or brain teasers.

sampleQuestions.title: Merge overlapping time intervals from multiple sources
sampleQuestions.prompt: A practical version of a classic: merge availability windows coming from several unsynchronised systems, with clock skew.
keyPointsToCover: Sort by start, then sweep
The clock-skew tolerance as an explicit parameter you ask about
Edge cases: zero-length intervals, exact touching boundaries

provenance.value: Uber describes its coding exercises as real-world problems.

Exact versus approximate distinct counts and when approximation is acceptable
Downsampling and retention tiers

qaBank.question: How is an Uber coding interview actually structured?

provenance.value: Uber published the internal breakdown of the hour on its engineering blog.

answer.approach: Uber is one of the only companies that published how the hour is divided. Budget your time against their published split, not a guess.
keyPoints: About an hour with each interviewer
Introduction, then a coding exercise of 30-40 minutes
Then 5-10 minutes on your past experience
Then 5-10 minutes for your questions
Onsite is up to six of these back-to-back, with short breaks and a longer lunch break
pitfalls: Spending 15 minutes on the intro and losing the coding time
Treating the experience discussion as small talk - it is a published part of the evaluation
Having no questions ready for a published 5-10 minute slot
followUps: Are there brain teasers? Uber states explicitly that it avoids logic puzzles and brain teasers.
What exactly is scored? Approach and communication, Big O, naming, edge cases, iteration.

rounds.name: Phone interview

structureClaim.value: One or two phone interviews, typically 20 to 45 minutes each, covering background and interest plus a technical coding question for engineering roles.

rounds.focusSummary: Whether you can work through a coding question while narrating, with no visual channel at all.

greenFlags: Narrates the approach before typing

Implement it correctly before optimising
Say what you would change if the input grew by a factor of a thousand

provenance.value: Palantir publishes start simple and then expand as its own phone-interview advice.

Palantir publishes what candidates commonly ask at the end: what Palantir does, what the interviewer works on, what it is like to be new there, and how the internship programme is structured.

rounds.name: Writing good code

structureClaim.value: Palantir publishes a dedicated guide for this competency, defining good code as efficient, effective, and easy to read, maintain and upgrade.

rounds.focusSummary: Translating a conceptual algorithmic solution into code that actually implements it - Palantir names this as a core facet of a good coding interview.

whatTheyLookFor: Code that runs at optimal performance and can be scaled
greenFlags: Thinks past the O() bound to constant factors - Palantir gives the n versus 2n loop example itself
redFlags: Unnecessary O(n) space where none was needed

whatTheyLookFor: Free of bugs and easy to test
greenFlags: Names edge cases and how they would be tested
redFlags: No thought given to how the code would be verified

evaluationRubric.category: Easy to read, maintain and upgrade
whatTheyLookFor: Properly structured and defined elements, from variable naming to file, class and framework structure
greenFlags: Names and structure that a stranger could follow
redFlags: Correct code nobody else could modify

whatTheyLookFor: Understanding what each library call does and at what complexity
greenFlags: States the complexity of a library call they used
redFlags: Calling a sort inside a loop without noticing

sampleQuestions.title: Implement a correct solution, then reduce the constant factor
sampleQuestions.prompt: Palantir uses this exact example: sometimes an O(n) algorithm can be implemented either with a loop that does n or 2n iterations, and sometimes an O(n) space data structure is unnecessary overhead.
keyPointsToCover: Reach the optimal asymptotic complexity
Then find the second pass you can eliminate
Then ask whether the auxiliary structure is needed at all

provenance.value: Palantir publishes exactly this example in its Writing Good Code guide.

insiderTips.value: Palantir publishes which languages are acceptable: any imperative language including Java, Python, C/C++, C#, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Groovy and TypeScript. Non-imperative languages such as Prolog, Lisp and Erlang are not acceptable, and neither are Cobol or Fortran.
insiderTips.quote: we will not be okay with non-imperative languages (Prolog, Lisp, Erlang) or languages that are too exotic, ancient and/or different from modern industry practices (Cobol, Fortran)

insiderTips.value: Palantir says it will not ask about tricky or obscure features of a specific language - it is interested in your skill as a coder, not your memory of the Java compiler.
Be prepared to code on a whiteboard onsite. Pen and paper or a computer are available on request.

rounds.name: Analyzing the efficiency of code

structureClaim.value: A published competency: analysing and improving efficiency so code runs with optimal complexity, and building systems that store and transmit data efficiently.

rounds.focusSummary: Not just Big O. Palantir asks which components in a large system are critical for efficiency and where trade-offs can be made.

whatTheyLookFor: Correct calculation, and understanding how performance differs across values
greenFlags: Distinguishes best, worst and average cases and says which matters here
redFlags: Reciting a memorised bound without deriving it

whatTheyLookFor: Knowing when trading space for time helps and when it is pure overhead
greenFlags: Explicitly weighs the auxiliary structure against the gain
redFlags: Only ever discussing time

whatTheyLookFor: The practical effect of an optimisation that does not change the order of complexity
Knowing when a workload is processor bound versus I/O bound
greenFlags: Asks where the bottleneck actually is before optimising
redFlags: Optimising the part that is not the constraint

sampleQuestions.title: Which data would you keep in memory on a very high-memory server, and how?
sampleQuestions.prompt: Palantir poses this question itself: how can we take advantage of servers with very high memory by keeping part of the data in memory for fast access - what data do we keep, how will it be synchronised, and how can it be accessed most efficiently?
keyPointsToCover: Which slice of the data is hot, and how you would measure that
Synchronisation and invalidation strategy
Access structure for the query pattern
When replicating data in multiple storage formats beats optimising for space

provenance.value: Palantir poses this exact set of questions in its efficiency guide.

insiderTips.value: Palantir asks when processor-time optimisation is critical and when performance is I/O bound. Have an answer for both.

rounds.name: Navigating open-ended questions

structureClaim.value: A published competency: tackling technical challenges that are open-ended, with multiple possible solutions incurring different trade-offs.
structureClaim.quote: At Palantir, we rarely work on problems that have a single optimal solution.

rounds.focusSummary: Palantir says the problems it tackles transcend purely technical definitions and that perfect solutions do not exist. Pragmatism is scored.

whatTheyLookFor: Multiple approaches with different consequences named
greenFlags: Lays out two or three options and the cost of each
redFlags: One approach presented as the only one

whatTheyLookFor: Arriving at a concrete approach; Palantir says deliver a functioning idea first, then expand it
greenFlags: Commits to something buildable and says what it defers
redFlags: Exploring forever without converging

whatTheyLookFor: Solving with limited time and resources where perfect is unattainable
greenFlags: Names the constraint that forced the compromise
redFlags: Designing for an unconstrained world

sampleQuestions.title: Enable a workflow for which no ideal solution exists
sampleQuestions.prompt: Palantir lists this as one of the four shapes of open-ended problem it works on, alongside building a complex system from scratch, introducing a new solution into a large existing codebase, and solving a problem with limited time and resources.
keyPointsToCover: Establish what good enough means before designing
Name two or three approaches with their different trade-offs
Commit to one and state explicitly what it does not solve
Say what you would build first to learn the most

provenance.value: Palantir publishes these four problem shapes in its open-ended questions guide.

insiderTips.value: Palantir preparation advice is to build real things that solve real problems, and to analyse existing technology by picking an app and working out the technical challenges its developers must have hit.
Remember the framing Palantir gives: solutions that work before we have time to make them perfect.

rounds.name: Working inside existing systems

rounds.focusSummary: Making confident, informed decisions about how to fix a bug or add a feature without perfect understanding of the whole system.

whatTheyLookFor: Forming hypotheses about structure and testing them, rather than reading every line
greenFlags: Says what they expect to find, then checks
redFlags: Linear reading from the top of the file

whatTheyLookFor: Resisting the urge to rewrite; Palantir explicitly tells candidates to reject that urge
greenFlags: Works with the code as it exists to add the feature cleanly
redFlags: This is bad, it should be rewritten

whatTheyLookFor: Understanding the potential risks of a change and how to eliminate them without reading everything
greenFlags: Considers the blast radius of the fix
redFlags: Fixing the symptom and breaking something else

whatTheyLookFor: Asking afterwards whether you did a good job
greenFlags: Notes the warning or failing test that would have found it sooner
redFlags: Declaring victory at the first green run

Use depth-first and breadth-first exploration deliberately - Palantir names both
Verify the fix did not break something else

Name what could go wrong with your mitigation

qaBank.question: Which programming languages can I actually use in a Palantir interview?

provenance.value: Palantir publishes its language rules in the Writing Good Code guide.

answer.approach: Palantir is the only company here that publishes a language allow-list and a deny-list. Use it.
keyPoints: Acceptable: any imperative language - Java, Python, C/C++, C#, JavaScript, and variations like Rust, Go, Groovy, TypeScript
Also acceptable: older imperative languages such as Visual Basic, Pascal/Delphi, Perl
Not acceptable: non-imperative languages - Prolog, Lisp, Erlang
Not acceptable: exotic or ancient languages far from modern industry practice - Cobol, Fortran
Palantir also says it will not ask about tricky or obscure features of a specific language
pitfalls: Choosing a functional language you are strongest in and finding it is excluded
Preparing language trivia that Palantir states it will not ask about

answer.approach: Because it has been rewritten three times specifically so that a strong model cannot solve it for you - and Anthropic published exactly how.

Version 3: after Claude Opus 4.5 matched human performance on version 2, they switched to puzzle-solving on a tiny, heavily constrained instruction set, comparable to a Zachtronics game
The current design targets problems sufficiently out of distribution that human reasoning can beat training-data advantage
They deliberately did not ban AI - engineer Tristan Hume wanted a setting where people could distinguish themselves with AI, as on the job
pitfalls: Preparing familiar optimisation recipes - the design intent is that none of them transfer
Expecting a conventional take-home shape

qaBank.question: What does LinkedIn actually publish about its hiring process?

provenance.value: Taken from the LinkedIn How We Hire page.

answer.approach: Four stages, one structural detail that matters, and an honest warning about speed.
keyPoints: Application - reviewed against the basic and some preferred qualifications on the job description
Conversation - a recruiter call, then possibly a video call with the hiring manager or a team member covering technical expertise
Interview - multiple team members, each focusing on a different skill area, with case studies or whiteboard exercises depending on role
Decision - assessing potential to succeed in the job, which may take several weeks
LinkedIn frames the whole thing as a fair, inclusive and transparent process
pitfalls: Repeating the same story to every interviewer when each covers a different skill area
Expecting a fast decision - LinkedIn says several weeks outright
followUps: Which skill areas? Not published - ask the recruiter, since the structure itself is published.

qaBank.question: What should I study for a LinkedIn system design round?

provenance.value: Derived from the systems LinkedIn built, open-sourced and documented itself.

answer.approach: LinkedIn wrote a lot of the infrastructure it runs on and then open-sourced it. Read those write-ups rather than generic design material.
keyPoints: Kafka - the distributed commit log originated at LinkedIn
Pinot - real-time analytics at massive scale, built and open-sourced there
Venice - the derived data platform, open-sourced with a published write-up
Brooklin - near real-time data streaming, open-sourced
TonY - distributed training framework contributed to LF AI & Data Foundation
The common thread: precompute offline, serve online, keep the stream as the source of truth
pitfalls: Designing a synchronous read path for a social graph at scale
Ignoring the derived-data pattern that most of the product actually relies on
followUps: Where are these documented? The LinkedIn Engineering open-source pages and blog.

qaBank.question: What should I study for a LinkedIn system design round?

provenance.value: Derived from the systems LinkedIn built, open-sourced and documented itself.

answer.approach: LinkedIn wrote a lot of the infrastructure it runs on and then open-sourced it. Read those write-ups rather than generic design material.
keyPoints: Kafka - the distributed commit log originated at LinkedIn
Pinot - real-time analytics at massive scale, built and open-sourced there
Venice - the derived data platform, open-sourced with a published write-up
Brooklin - near real-time data streaming, open-sourced
TonY - distributed training framework contributed to LF AI & Data Foundation
The common thread: precompute offline, serve online, keep the stream as the source of truth
pitfalls: Designing a synchronous read path for a social graph at scale
Ignoring the derived-data pattern that most of the product actually relies on
followUps: Where are these documented? The LinkedIn Engineering open-source pages and blog.

qaBank.question: How long will Airbnb take to respond, and what are my odds?

provenance.value: Airbnb publishes both the response target and the application volume in its candidate FAQ.

answer.approach: Airbnb is unusually candid about the funnel, which is more useful than a vague reassurance.
keyPoints: Airbnb aims to respond within three to four weeks, either way
It reviews about 15,000 applications each month
It states plainly that meeting the listed qualifications does not guarantee an interview
The process varies by position and may include taking a test, making a video, or joining an event
Candidates typically meet multiple team members to ensure mutual fit
pitfalls: Reading a rejection as a signal about your qualifications - Airbnb says outright that volume is the constraint
Not asking which of the three named formats applies to you
followUps: Is there a decision SLA later in the process? No - only the application-stage target is published.

qaBank.question: Will Airbnb sponsor a visa or hire me anywhere?

provenance.value: Airbnb publishes its work-authorisation and location constraints in its candidate FAQ.

answer.approach: Check this before you invest in the process. Airbnb is specific and restrictive.
keyPoints: For the most part Airbnb only considers applicants already legally able to work in the country the job is based in
Visa sponsorship is described as very rare and only for specialised positions
Airbnb also names US states where employees cannot be located: Alaska, Mississippi and North Dakota
These are published constraints, not recruiter discretion
pitfalls: Assuming a remote-friendly company has no location constraints
Applying broadly across countries without checking authorisation
followUps: Where is this stated? The Airbnb Careers FAQ, in its own words.

qaBank.question: What should I read before an Airbnb design round?

provenance.value: Derived from the sections Airbnb publishes on its own tech blog and open-source site.

answer.approach: Airbnb publishes its engineering by section. Read the section matching the team you are interviewing into.
keyPoints: The tech blog is organised into mobile, infrastructure, fintech, data, AI and ML, web and open source
Data-platform and workflow-orchestration material is the most distinctive
Trust and fraud is a first-class engineering concern with its own advertised org
The marketplace is two-sided - design answers that only consider guests miss half of it
Booking correctness, not scale, is usually the hard part of the domain
pitfalls: Designing a generic e-commerce checkout for a marketplace with inventory that cannot be duplicated
Ignoring abuse and fraud in a product built on stranger-to-stranger trust
followUps: Is the round composition published? No - Airbnb publishes the funnel, not the loop.

qaBank.question: What does ByteDance say strong candidates actually do?

provenance.value: ByteDance publishes this observation directly in its interview-tips page.

answer.approach: ByteDance published its own observation of what separates strong candidates, which is effectively a checklist. Very few companies do this.
keyPoints: Ask relevant questions before writing the code
Diagram the problem
Validate their assumptions
Check their work constantly without being prompted
Pay attention to efficiency without making the solution unnecessarily complicated
ByteDance also states the interviewer is more interested in your thought process than the final answer
pitfalls: Coding immediately from the prompt with no clarification
Waiting to be asked whether your solution works
Over-engineering in pursuit of efficiency
followUps: Where should I practise? ByteDance names HackerRank and Nowcoder specifically.
How many interviews? Two to three, each 30 minutes to an hour.

qaBank.question: What is the ByteDance interview loop?

provenance.value: ByteDance publishes the count, the length and who you meet.

answer.approach: Short by large-company standards, and ByteDance publishes the shape.
keyPoints: Two to three interviews
Each typically 30 minutes to an hour
You usually speak with potential teammates, cross-functional colleagues and your hiring manager
Technical rounds cover coding, algorithms and design plus team-specific technologies
Non-technical rounds use behavioural, hypothetical and case-based questions
pitfalls: Preparing for a six-round FAANG-style loop that does not exist here
Neglecting the hypothetical and case-based modes
followUps: Is there a timeline? Not published - ask your recruiter.

qaBank.question: What are the five qualities ByteDance looks for?

provenance.value: ByteDance names all five on its interview-tips page.

answer.approach: Five named qualities. Map one story to each before the loop.
keyPoints: A strong desire to achieve excellence
A spirit for collaboration
An 'Always Day 1' attitude
An ability to communicate candidly and openly
A passion for technology
ByteDance tells you directly to review your experiences for stories demonstrating these
pitfalls: Missing 'Always Day 1', which is the least self-explanatory of the five
Hedged answers, when candour is explicitly one of the five
followUps: How formal is it? ByteDance says the interview is meant to be a conversation rather than a question-and-answer session.
